analysis.one_liner: Writes the FTC's click-to-cancel rule into law so subscription customers can cancel as easily as they signed up.
analysis.headline: The Click to Cancel Act has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since it was introduced with 19 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, with no committee vote or floor action scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The Federal Trade Commission issued a rule in 2024 requiring companies to make canceling a subscription as easy as signing up — for example, letting you cancel online if you subscribed online, and ending surprise renewals after free trials. A federal appeals court struck that rule down before it took effect, so it currently has no legal force. This bill would write the rule into federal law, making it binding and enforceable by the FTC the same way other consumer protection rules are.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who subscribes to anything: streaming services, gym memberships, meal kits, phone apps, subscription boxes, and telecom services. The bill requires companies to let you cancel through the same medium you used to sign up, to get your clear consent before renewing after a free trial, and to remind you before an automatic renewal. Consumers who give up fighting with retention agents over the phone, or who get charged after forgetting a free trial, would stop paying for services they no longer want.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the FTC's November 2024 negative-option (click-to-cancel) rule the force of law, so companies must let consumers cancel subscriptions as easily as they enrolled [S2].
Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, so the FTC can enforce the rule with its full range of penalties and investigative powers [S2].

Codifying the rule in statute matters because the FTC's own rule was struck down by a federal appeals court in July 2025 before it could take effect; a statute would put the cancellation requirements back on firm legal footing.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that sell subscriptions — gyms, streaming platforms, meal-kit and app companies, telecom providers — would bear compliance costs: building one-click cancellation, sending renewal reminders, obtaining explicit consent after free trials, and losing revenue from customers who would have kept paying simply because canceling was a hassle. Some firms argue this would discourage free-trial offers.

drawbacks.text: Subscription businesses argue the compliance burden is real: they must redesign signup and cancellation flows, send reminders, and track consent, and some say the result will be fewer free trials and higher subscription prices to cover the costs [S2].

A portion of the revenue subscription companies collect today comes from customers who no longer want the service but fail to cancel; ending that revenue stream is a genuine cost to those firms and may be passed on to the customers who do stay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers — not paying indefinitely for services they tried to quit — is direct and widespread, since the average household juggles multiple subscriptions. The costs fall on businesses and are the ordinary cost of honest dealing; the bill simply forbids making cancellation harder than signup. The main honest caveat is that some free-trial promotions may shrink, and compliance costs may show up in prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the Click to Cancel Act on July 29, 2025, with Reps. Magaziner and Deluzio as original sponsors [S1].
The bill had 19 cosponsors, all Democrats, as of the most recent listing [S3].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and the full action history shows no markup, no vote, and no further movement since [S4].

The bill's entire text is the codification of the FTC's November 2024 Negative Option Rule, which a federal appeals court vacated before its effective date, leaving the cancellation protections without legal force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, subscription businesses that earn revenue from customers who can't easily cancel: with the FTC's rule struck down and the bill stalled in committee, no cancellation requirements are in force. Consumers remain stuck with the status quo of phone-call gauntlets and surprise renewals.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the FTC's click-to-cancel rule as law

for.name: Reps. Magaziner and Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since it was referred on the day of introduction

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on, so the bill's support so far is entirely one-party [S3].

industries.industry: Subscription-based businesses (gyms, streaming, meal kits, apps, subscription boxes)
industries.note: The bill would force them to make cancellation as easy as signup and end surprise renewals, eliminating revenue from customers who would otherwise keep paying out of friction or forgetfulness. Their interest in defeating or stalling the bill runs directly against consumers' interest in easy cancellation.

industries.industry: Telecom and media companies with auto-renewing plans
industries.note: Auto-renewal and hard-to-cancel plans are core to retention economics in these industries; the rule would require clear consent and easy exit paths, cutting into that revenue.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a one-line codification with no Republican cosponsors and no committee movement since introduction. Most bills at this stage — referred to committee, no hearing, no bipartisan support — die quietly at the end of the Congress. Its chances improve only if the Energy and Commerce Committee schedules a markup, which has not happened and is not scheduled.
